title: The Two Substances and the Work of Separation
arc: From the beginning two substances stand opposed — Light and Darkness, the beautiful and the bitter, life and death — and the whole spiritual labor consists in separating the beautiful forth from the Darkness.
reading:
This short chapter (numbered 120, "Concerning the Two Substances") states the foundational dualism on which the whole teaching of correspondences rests, and then names the redemptive operation that follows from it. Read in correspondence, the "two substances existing from the beginning" are not two co-eternal cosmic stuffs in a metaphysical sense, but the two essences that the soul finds always before it: the Divine — love and wisdom proceeding from the Father of Greatness — and the proprium, the self-love that opposes it. Light is wisdom / Divine Truth; Darkness is falsity from evil, the absence of that light. They are "from the beginning" because, for any soul that exists, both poles are already given: the influx of the Lord on one side, and the inherited self-love that resists it on the other.

The teaching then sharpens the contrast through three correspondential pairs that all name the same polarity at different registers. Light against Darkness names it intellectually, as truth against falsity. The beautiful (ⲡⲉⲧⲁⲛⲓⲧ) against the bitter (ⲥⲁϣⲉ) names it on the side of affection and taste — the sweetness of divine good against the bitterness that the soul receives from the corrupt tree. And life against death (ⲡⲙⲟⲩ) names it as the ultimate state: conjunction with the Lord versus spiritual non-being. The triple naming is not redundant; it shows that the same opposition runs through every degree of the human — through understanding, through will, and through life itself.

The closing line gives the practical point of the whole chapter: "separating the beautiful one forth from the Darkness" (ⲛ̄ⲡⲱⲣⲭ ⲡⲡⲉⲧⲁⲛⲓⲧ ⲁⲃⲁⲗ ⲙ̄ⲡⲕⲉⲕⲉ). The verb ⲡⲱⲣⲭ is the technical word for the discriminative work of regeneration — distinguishing truth from falsity, separating what belongs to the Lord from what belongs to self-love. So the doctrinal statement (two substances) immediately turns into a doctrine of regeneration: because the soul stands in mingling, the Lord's work in it is to draw the beautiful out of the bitter, the living out of the dead, the light out of the darkness. The teaching thus moves in one short arc from the metaphysical premise of the two essences, through their threefold expression as truth/affection/life, to the single redemptive operation that the rest of the Kephalaia will unfold: separation, the un-mingling of what was joined.
